On October 25, 2026, we released out-of-band security updates for .NET 8.0.33, .NET 9.0.22, .NET 10.0.14, and .NET 11 Release Candidate 3 (prerelease). We recommend updating affected applications and build environments as soon as possible. .NET Framework is not affected.

## Release Notes

* [Release details and feedback](https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/10660)
* [.NET 8.0.33 and .NET SDK 8.0.133 / 8.0.427](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/8.0/8.0.33/8.0.33.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/8.0))
* [.NET 9.0.22 and .NET SDK 9.0.123 / 9.0.320](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/9.0/9.0.22/9.0.22.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/9.0))
* [.NET 10.0.14 and .NET SDK 10.0.114 / 10.0.403](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/10.0/10.0.14/10.0.14.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/10.0))
* [.NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 and .NET SDK 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 (prerelease)](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc3/11.0.0-rc.3.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0))

## Security advisories

| Advisory | Applicability | Announcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [CVE-2026-111497](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-p3jp-9v83-76w9) | Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write; all platforms when processing untrusted Brotli data. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494) |
| [CVE-2026-114148](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/security/advisories/GHSA-r6pf-x897-gm86) | Linux archive ownership; distribution-specific ASP.NET Core archives and source-build engineering inputs. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/495) |
| [CVE-2026-70197](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-4mpw-cpwj-hxxj) | Windows sockets memory corruption; corrected October 13 fix. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/493) |
| [CVE-2026-102870](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/security/advisories/GHSA-g27p-qf6j-c96c) | Standalone Blazor WebAssembly debugger packages on .NET 10/11; corrected October 13 fix. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/492) |

The October 13 updates did not fully address CVE-2026-70197 and CVE-2026-102870. These out-of-band updates provide the corrected fixes; the original advisory identities and revision history are preserved. For CVE-2026-102870, update the affected standalone Server/DevServer package references; updating only the shared runtime is not a substitute.

For CVE-2026-114148, affected Microsoft-published .NET 8/9 ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarball installations require a clean replacement following the advisory. Source-built archives are build/engineering inputs, not directly deployed production runtimes. Update those inputs and recreate their extracted workspaces using ownership-controlled extraction; review and rebuild affected downstream outputs as needed. .NET 10/11 applicability is limited to source-built distributions.

Also announced at [.NET October 2026 Out-of-Band Security Updates](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/dotnet-october-2026-oob-security-updates/).

Please use the [release feedback issue](https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/10660) for release-wide issues and the linked per-CVE discussions for advisory questions.

<!-- dotnet-oob-rollup:2026-10-25 -->

## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- ASP.NET Core 8 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 8 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 9 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 ASP.NET Core 9 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 These products use the archive names `aspnetcore-runtime-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, `aspnetcore-runtime-composite-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, and `aspnetcore-targeting-pack-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, where `{rid}` is `linux-arm`, `linux-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-musl-arm`, `linux-musl-arm64` or `linux-musl-x64`. Runtime tarballs are listed on the [.NET download site](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet); targeting-pack tarballs are distributed through the .NET download CDN. ### Source-built distributions Every tarball type produced by source-build is affected in the ranges below, not only SDK tarballs. The versions in this table identify the corresponding source-build SDK release. Source-built tarballs are used in build and engineering workflows, rather than deployed directly to customer installations. Consuming an affected source-build archive does not, by itself, mean that a production shared runtime was installed from that archive. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- Source-built .NET 8 Linux distributions | >= 8.0.100, < 8.0.133 | 8.0.133 Source-built .NET 9 Linux distributions | >= 9.0.100, < 9.0.123 | 9.0.123 Source-built .NET 10.0.1xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.113 | 10.0.114-servicing.26522.126 Source-built .NET 10.0.4xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.400, <= 10.0.402 | 10.0.403-servicing.26523.112 Source-built .NET 11 preview Linux distributions | >= 11.0.100-preview.1.26104.118, <= 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. This advisory also provides guidance on updating affected installations and source-build engineering workflows. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- ASP.NET Core 8 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 8 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 9 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 ASP.NET Core 9 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 These products use the archive names `aspnetcore-runtime-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, `aspnetcore-runtime-composite-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, and `aspnetcore-targeting-pack-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, where `{rid}` is `linux-arm`, `linux-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-musl-arm`, `linux-musl-arm64` or `linux-musl-x64`. Runtime tarballs are listed on the [.NET download site](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet); targeting-pack tarballs are distributed through the .NET download CDN. ### Source-built distributions Every tarball type produced by source-build is affected in the ranges below, not only SDK tarballs. The versions in this table identify the corresponding source-build SDK release. Source-built tarballs are used in build and engineering workflows, rather than deployed directly to customer installations. Consuming an affected source-build archive does not, by itself, mean that a production shared runtime was installed from that archive. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- Source-built .NET 8 Linux distributions | >= 8.0.100, < 8.0.133 | 8.0.133 Source-built .NET 9 Linux distributions | >= 9.0.100, < 9.0.123 | 9.0.123 Source-built .NET 10.0.1xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.113 | 10.0.114-servicing.26522.126 Source-built .NET 10.0.4xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.400, <= 10.0.402 | 10.0.403-servicing.26523.112 Source-built .NET 11 preview Linux distributions | >= 11.0.100-preview.1.26104.118, <= 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. For a shared or privileged installation, run extraction in the trusted administrator context. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Check the actual runtime selected by each application, not only the version reported by an unrelated `dotnet` executable on `PATH`. Ensure that no service, scheduled job, or runtime search path still selects the affected installation. Retire the old tree using your deployment procedures, preserving evidence first if compromise is suspected. 6. Rebuild affected custom container images from trusted inputs using the patched archives and ownership-controlled extraction, and deploy replacement containers. Changing only a running container does not correct the image used to create subsequent containers. #### Source-build engineering workflows If a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built tarball, update that input to the patched source-build release listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Recreate its extracted workspace in a new, trusted directory using ownership-controlled extraction, rather than reusing a tree extracted from the affected archive. The extraction guidance above also applies to these workspaces. Review downstream runtime or SDK packages and custom images for ownership inherited from the affected archive, and rebuild affected outputs as needed. The customer-installation steps above apply if affected outputs were actually installed or deployed; do not treat the source-build engineering archive itself as a deployed production runtime. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. This advisory also provides guidance on updating affected installations and source-build engineering workflows. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- ASP.NET Core 8 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 8 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 9 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 ASP.NET Core 9 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 These products use the archive names `aspnetcore-runtime-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, `aspnetcore-runtime-composite-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, and `aspnetcore-targeting-pack-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, where `{rid}` is `linux-arm`, `linux-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-musl-arm`, `linux-musl-arm64` or `linux-musl-x64`. Runtime tarballs are listed on the [.NET download site](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet); targeting-pack tarballs are distributed through the .NET download CDN. ### Source-built distributions Every tarball type produced by source-build is affected in the ranges below, not only SDK tarballs. The versions in this table identify the corresponding source-build SDK release. Source-built tarballs are used in build and engineering workflows, rather than deployed directly to customer installations. Consuming an affected source-build archive does not, by itself, mean that a production shared runtime was installed from that archive. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- Source-built .NET 8 Linux distributions | >= 8.0.100, < 8.0.133 | 8.0.133 Source-built .NET 9 Linux distributions | >= 9.0.100, < 9.0.123 | 9.0.123 Source-built .NET 10.0.1xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.113 | 10.0.114-servicing.26522.126 Source-built .NET 10.0.4xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.400, <= 10.0.402 | 10.0.403-servicing.26523.112 Source-built .NET 11 preview Linux distributions | >= 11.0.100-preview.1.26104.118, <= 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. For a shared or privileged installation, run extraction in the trusted administrator context. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Check the actual runtime selected by each application, not only the version reported by an unrelated `dotnet` executable on `PATH`. Ensure that no service, scheduled job, or runtime search path still selects the affected installation. Retire the old tree using your deployment procedures, preserving evidence first if compromise is suspected. 6. Rebuild affected custom container images from trusted inputs using the patched archives and ownership-controlled extraction, and deploy replacement containers. Changing only a running container does not correct the image used to create subsequent containers. #### Source-build engineering workflows If a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built tarball, update that input to the patched source-build release listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Recreate its extracted workspace in a new, trusted directory using ownership-controlled extraction, rather than reusing a tree extracted from the affected archive. The extraction guidance above also applies to these workspaces. Review downstream runtime or SDK packages and custom images for ownership inherited from the affected archive, and rebuild affected outputs as needed. The customer-installation steps above apply if affected outputs were actually installed or deployed; do not treat the source-build engineering archive itself as a deployed production runtime. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages listed below. ### .NET 8 Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | --------------- ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. This advisory also provides guidance on updating affected installations and source-build engineering workflows. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- ASP.NET Core 8 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 8 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 9 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 ASP.NET Core 9 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 These products use the archive names `aspnetcore-runtime-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, `aspnetcore-runtime-composite-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, and `aspnetcore-targeting-pack-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, where `{rid}` is `linux-arm`, `linux-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-musl-arm`, `linux-musl-arm64` or `linux-musl-x64`. Runtime tarballs are listed on the [.NET download site](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet); targeting-pack tarballs are distributed through the .NET download CDN. ### Source-built distributions Every tarball type produced by source-build is affected in the ranges below, not only SDK tarballs. The versions in this table identify the corresponding source-build SDK release. Source-built tarballs are used in build and engineering workflows, rather than deployed directly to customer installations. Consuming an affected source-build archive does not, by itself, mean that a production shared runtime was installed from that archive. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- Source-built .NET 8 Linux distributions | >= 8.0.100, < 8.0.133 | 8.0.133 Source-built .NET 9 Linux distributions | >= 9.0.100, < 9.0.123 | 9.0.123 Source-built .NET 10.0.1xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.113 | 10.0.114-servicing.26522.126 Source-built .NET 10.0.4xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.400, <= 10.0.402 | 10.0.403-servicing.26523.112 Source-built .NET 11 preview Linux distributions | >= 11.0.100-preview.1.26104.118, <= 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. For a shared or privileged installation, run extraction in the trusted administrator context. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Check the actual runtime selected by each application, not only the version reported by an unrelated `dotnet` executable on `PATH`. Ensure that no service, scheduled job, or runtime search path still selects the affected installation. Retire the old tree using your deployment procedures, preserving evidence first if compromise is suspected. 6. Rebuild affected custom container images from trusted inputs using the patched archives and ownership-controlled extraction, and deploy replacement containers. Changing only a running container does not correct the image used to create subsequent containers. #### Source-build engineering workflows If a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built tarball, update that input to the patched source-build release listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Recreate its extracted workspace in a new, trusted directory using ownership-controlled extraction, rather than reusing a tree extracted from the affected archive. The extraction guidance above also applies to these workspaces. Review downstream runtime or SDK packages and custom images for ownership inherited from the affected archive, and rebuild affected outputs as needed. The customer-installation steps above apply if affected outputs were actually installed or deployed; do not treat the source-build engineering archive itself as a deployed production runtime. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See [mitigations](#mitigations) for the affected usage paths and default settings. ### How do I fix the issue? Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above. .NET release | Runtime | SDK versions ------------ | ------- | ------------ .NET 8 | 8.0.33 | 8.0.133, 8.0.427 .NET 9 | 9.0.22 | 9.0.123, 9.0.320 .NET 10 | 10.0.14 | 10.0.114, 10.0.403 .NET 11 previews | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.33 Runtime or .NET 8.0.133 or 8.0.427 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.22 Runtime or .NET 9.0.123 or 9.0.320 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.14 Runtime or .NET 10.0.114 or 10.0.403 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0. Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect. If you have deployed [self-contained applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments), rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime. For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Events.RelatedBody: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. This advisory also provides guidance on updating affected installations and source-build engineering workflows. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. For a shared or privileged installation, run extraction in the trusted administrator context. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Check the actual runtime selected by each application, not only the version reported by an unrelated `dotnet` executable on `PATH`. Ensure that no service, scheduled job, or runtime search path still selects the affected installation. Retire the old tree using your deployment procedures, preserving evidence first if compromise is suspected. 6. Rebuild affected custom container images from trusted inputs using the patched archives and ownership-controlled extraction, and deploy replacement containers. Changing only a running container does not correct the image used to create subsequent containers. #### Source-build engineering workflows If a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built tarball, update that input to the patched source-build release listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Recreate its extracted workspace in a new, trusted directory using ownership-controlled extraction, rather than reusing a tree extracted from the affected archive. The extraction guidance above also applies to these workspaces. Review downstream runtime or SDK packages and custom images for ownership inherited from the affected archive, and rebuild affected outputs as needed. The customer-installation steps above apply if affected outputs were actually installed or deployed; do not treat the source-build engineering archive itself as a deployed production runtime. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? You are affected if your application uses an affected Brotli decoder included in a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), including a decoder linked into a NativeAOT application, to decompress attacker-controlled data. See [mitigations](#mitigations) for the affected usage paths and default settings. ### How do I fix the issue? Install the updated runtime or SDK for the .NET version used by your application. If your application directly references an affected package, update that reference to the patched version listed above. .NET release | Runtime | SDK versions ------------ | ------- | ------------ .NET 8 | 8.0.33 | 8.0.133, 8.0.427 .NET 9 | 9.0.22 | 9.0.123, 9.0.320 .NET 10 | 10.0.14 | 10.0.114, 10.0.403 .NET 11 previews | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 Download .NET from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.33 Runtime or .NET 8.0.133 or 8.0.427 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.22 Runtime or .NET 9.0.123 or 9.0.320 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.14 Runtime or .NET 10.0.114 or 10.0.403 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0. Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect. If you have deployed [self-contained applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments), rebuild and redeploy those applications with the updated runtime. For NativeAOT applications, update the SDK and any explicit compiler or runtime-pack references to patched versions, then republish and redeploy the application. Updating the machine's shared runtime alone does not replace a decoder already linked into a NativeAOT executable. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Events.RelatedBody: ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Issues.Title: [release/3.1] Reset current_no_gc_region_info after leaving no gc region implicitly
Issues.Body:
Backport https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/73602.

## Customer Impact
Customers reported occasional `System.InvalidOperationException` with message `The NoGCRegion mode was already in progress` when calling `GC.TryStartNoGCRegion`. This is preventing them from using this optimization and impacting their cold start latencies.

## Testing
Customers have tried the fix on .NET 6 overnight and reported the exception never appears again. Meanwhile, there is an unpatched machine and observed 72 exceptions of the same type in the same time interval, proving this does fix the bug.

## Risk
Low. This only impact customer using `TryStartNoGCRegion`, and this is the right thing to do.
